etymologies.etymologyHTML: Variant of clew (“a ball of thread or yarn”), from Middle English clewe, from Old English clīewen (“ball”), from Proto-West Germanic *kliuwīn, from Proto-Germanic *kliuwīną, *klewô (“ball, bale”), from Proto-Indo-European *glew- (“to amass, conglomerate; clump, ball, bale”). Sense evolution with reference to the one which the mythical Theseus used to guide him out of the Minotaur's labyrinth. More at clew.

definitions.definition: (now rare) A strand of yarn etc. as used to guide one through a labyrinth; something which points the way, a guide.

quote.text: she had even had in the past a small smug conviction that in the domestic labyrinth she always kept the clue.

definitions.definition: Information which may lead one to a certain point or conclusion.

quote.text: Black tracks on the magneto, a hairline crack in the flywheel casing, pitted points or a spitless exhaust — all are clues to potential conkouts

definitions.definition: An object or a kind of indication which may be used as evidence.
Insight or understanding ("to have a clue [about]" or "to have clue". See have a clue, clue stick)
To provide someone with information which they lack (often used with "in" or "up").

quote.citation: 2014, John Macgregor, The Antibiography of Ian Mcnulty:
quote.text: I stared into my mind for some image to clue me what to say but I saw only blackness there.

quote.citation: 1864, John McNeill Boyd, A Manual for Naval Cadets, page 444:
quote.text: If the lee-side of the sail were clued up, the risk would be small compared with what it would be were the sheet nearly aft and the whole sail full of wind on starting the tack.
